title: The identity control plane is getting crowded
dek: Okta pushes deeper into PAM and IGA, agent identity keeps moving into the IAM center, and session theft raises the bar for privileged authentication.
disclosure: AI-generated summary from linked sources. Verify important details at the source.

stories.title: Okta pushes deeper into PAM, IGA and ITDR
stories.summary: The strategic signal is bigger than any single feature: access governance, privileged access and threat response are converging into a common identity-security operating model.
stories.why: Teams that historically stitched together SSO, IGA and PAM should expect more overlap among vendors and more pressure to justify where each control should live.

stories.title: Agent governance and machine identity keep moving toward the IAM center
stories.summary: Identity platforms increasingly treat AI agents, workloads and machine identities as first-class IAM subjects rather than implementation edge cases.
stories.why: PAM programs should start defining ownership, credential lifecycle, authorization boundaries and kill-switch behavior for agent identities now.

stories.title: Session theft makes ‘MFA enabled’ an incomplete control statement
stories.summary: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing and token replay continue to demonstrate that a completed MFA challenge does not guarantee a safe privileged session.
stories.why: Measure privileged authentication quality: phishing resistance, device trust, token protection, session risk and revocation capability, not merely MFA enrollment.

title: The service account problem is becoming the agent identity problem
dek: AI agents are adding speed and autonomy to an identity class most organizations already struggle to inventory and govern.

stories.title: The old controls still matter, but the execution window is shrinking
stories.summary: Ownership, purpose, least privilege, credential rotation and recertification remain foundational. Autonomous agents make weak lifecycle controls fail faster.
stories.why: Treat agent identities as governed identities with explicit owners, scoped authority, short-lived credentials and observable action boundaries.
